claims.text: As-cast HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure consisting of a primary BCC matrix with nanoscale coherent secondary precipitates.

Microstructural descriptors such as precipitate size, precipitate distribution, phase fraction, and lattice distortion can serve as inputs to a machine-learning surrogate for predicting Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
The proposed surrogate will predict the specified properties significantly faster than full-scale simulations while retaining comparable accuracy.
SEM, XRD, and nanoindentation can rapidly quantify all of the proposed microstructural input metrics.
Coherent precipitates in the BCC matrix modulate dislocation motion.
The hierarchical heterostructure modulates local stress distribution.
Quantified precipitate and phase descriptors encode dislocation-pinning effects relevant to yielding.
The proposed descriptors encode stress-relaxation effects responsible for elasticity and fracture.
A surrogate using these descriptors can capture the underlying mechanical mechanisms without running computationally heavy atomistic or continuum simulations.
The surrogate will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture characteristics within roughly 10% of experimental measurements.
The surrogate will reduce prediction time by an order of magnitude relative to conventional simulations.
Direct DFT evaluation of alloy yield strength and fracture is generally beyond the reach of available implementations.
DFT, atomistic, and finite-element simulations may inadequately capture the influence of hierarchical microstructural features in HfNbTiVAl10.
Substantial thermal- or mechanical-processing-induced deviation from the as-cast heterostructure may compromise predictive accuracy.
Insufficient characterization resolution may compromise predictive accuracy by failing to capture important descriptors.
Prediction error and speed improvement will depend on experimental-data quality, characterization resolution, and heterostructural complexity.
Different processing histories may require additional model calibration.
The hypothesis is to be rejected if any surrogate prediction differs from experiment by more than ±10% or if the descriptors show no consistent correlation with the measured properties.
